recipe.history:
The bell pepper — in all its rainbow of red, yellow, orange, and green — is a New World fruit with origins in the tropical regions of Mexico and Central America, where Capsicum annuum has been cultivated for at least six thousand years. Indigenous peoples of the Americas developed an extraordinary diversity of peppers long before European contact, and when Spanish conquistadors carried seeds back to Europe in the late fifteenth century, the pepper spread with astonishing speed across the globe. It was Portuguese traders who introduced peppers to Asia and Africa, while Spanish colonists brought them throughout the Mediterranean. Today, roasted peppers are a cornerstone of Spanish, Italian, Turkish, and Hungarian cuisines — they appear as tapas, as antipasto, as stuffed preparations, as the essential base of romesco and ajvar and countless other sauces. The act of roasting transforms a pepper from something raw and slightly bitter into something silken, sweet, and smoke-kissed, a wholly different ingredient with a depth that raw peppers simply cannot match.

Roasted peppers arrived in the American burger imagination primarily through the influence of Southwestern and California cuisine in the 1980s and 1990s, when chefs began embracing bold, colorful ingredient combinations that prioritized visual exuberance alongside flavor complexity. The multicolor presentation of roasted rainbow peppers — their jewel-toned reds, golds, and greens fanned across a burger — introduced an aesthetic dimension to burger building that went beyond the traditional stack of beige and brown. Colorful heirloom tomatoes, popularized by the farmers market movement of the 1990s, reinforced this rainbow approach to burger topping. A burger that looks like a ball pit — joyful, colorful, chaotic with good things — is a burger that invites you to play with your food in the best possible sense. The Belcher children, who have spent considerable time contemplating both burgers and ball pits, would recognize this burger immediately as a kindred spirit.

I built this burger for my nephew's birthday party, partly because I wanted to make something the kids would find exciting and partly because I had been obsessing about roasted peppers all week. I roasted a full tray of red, yellow, and orange peppers until their skins blistered and blackened, then peeled them and let them cool in their own sweet juices. I made a quick pickled slaw in three colors — red cabbage, green cabbage, yellow bell pepper — and formed little crispy cheese balls from sharp cheddar that I panko-breaded and fried golden. The whole assembly looked like a celebration, like someone had upended a confetti cannon over a hamburger, but every single element was earning its place through flavor. The kids ate them with wide eyes and asked for seconds. The adults, who had been skeptically watching me fry cheese balls and roast peppers for two hours, ate them in silent reverence.

Medium rare is the ground from which all good burger philosophy grows, and this burger — exuberant and colorful as it is — rests on that foundation with absolute seriousness. The internal temperature of 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit is not a preference for the faint of heart but an understanding of meat science: at this temperature, the muscle fibers have begun to firm but have not yet expelled their moisture, the fat has rendered partially and flows through the patty like a river of richness, and the contrast between a seared exterior crust and a rosy interior is at its most dramatic and satisfying. A gray, overcooked patty beneath all these joyful, colorful toppings would be a tragedy — a hollow center to an otherwise exuberant creation. The rosy, juicy medium rare patty is what makes all the color and fun above it worth something.
ingredients: 1/2 cup mashed potato (from 1 medium russet, cooked and cooled)
1 large egg plus 1 for egg wash
For the fried cheddar cheese balls:
6 oz sharp cheddar cheese, cut into 3/4-inch cubes
6 slices American or cheddar cheese (for melting on patty)
1 cup mixed heirloom cherry tomatoes, halved (red, yellow, orange, green)
Mayonnaise or special sauce (mayo + ketchup + relish + dash of hot sauce)
instructions: 1. Make the potato buns: Combine yeast, warm milk, and sugar; let sit 5–10 minutes until foamy. In a stand mixer bowl, combine flour and salt. Add mashed potato, yeast mixture, egg, and softened butter. Knead with dough hook 8 minutes until smooth and slightly tacky.

2. Rise in an oiled bowl covered with plastic wrap for 1–1.5 hours until doubled. Divide into 6 portions, shape into tight rounds, place on parchment-lined sheet. Proof 45 minutes. Brush with egg wash and bake at 375°F for 16–18 minutes until golden. Cool completely.
3. Make the special sauce: Whisk together 1/2 cup mayonnaise, 2 tbsp ketchup, 1 tbsp sweet relish, 1 tsp yellow mustard, and a dash of hot sauce. Refrigerate until needed.

4. Roast the rainbow peppers: Preheat broiler to high. Place whole peppers on a foil-lined baking sheet. Broil, turning every 5 minutes, until skins are fully blackened and blistered on all sides, 15–20 minutes total. Transfer to a bowl, cover tightly with plastic wrap, and steam 15 minutes. Peel, seed, and slice into strips. Toss with olive oil, salt, and pepper. Reserve at room temperature.

5. Make the multicolor slaw: Toss shredded red cabbage, green cabbage, julienned yellow bell pepper, and shredded carrot together. Whisk apple cider vinegar, honey, mayonnaise, celery seed, and salt in a small bowl. Pour over slaw and toss to coat. Refrigerate at least 30 minutes.

6. Make the fried cheese balls: Set up a breading station: flour in one bowl, beaten eggs in a second, panko mixed with smoked paprika and garlic powder in a third. Dredge each cheddar cube in flour, dip in egg, then roll in seasoned panko, pressing to adhere. For a thicker coat, repeat the egg and panko steps. Freeze coated cheese balls 20 minutes.

7. Heat 2 inches of neutral oil to 375°F in a small heavy pot. Fry cheese balls in batches of 3–4, about 60–90 seconds each, until golden brown and crispy. Remove quickly with a slotted spoon before cheese bursts through. Drain on a wire rack.

8. Prepare and cook the patties: Form ground beef into 6 patties (about 4 oz each), 3/4 inch thick with a center dimple. Season with salt and pepper. Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking; add oil. Sear patties 3 minutes per side until a deep crust forms. Place a slice of cheese on each patty after flipping. Cook until internal temperature reaches 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare. Rest 3–4 minutes.
9. Toast buns cut-side down in a dry skillet 1–2 minutes until golden.

10. Assemble: Spread special sauce on both bun halves. Place the cheesy, rested patty on the bottom bun. Arrange strips of roasted rainbow peppers over the patty in a colorful fan. Pile a generous tangle of multicolor slaw on top. Scatter halved heirloom cherry tomatoes over the slaw. Perch 3–4 fried cheddar cheese balls on top of everything. Crown with the top bun and serve immediately while cheese balls are still hot and crispy.
